title: NASA Glenn Says Researchers Sent Photons Air-to-Ground Over a Quantum Channel in the US
summary: NASA Glenn Research Center posted on 4 Nov 2026 that researchers sent photons between an aircraft and a ground station over a quantum channel, calling it a US first; a 22 Oct LinkedIn post by Carolyn Mercer described witnessing an air-to-ground quantum entanglement demonstration at Glenn. No nasa.gov press release for this claim was found.
body: NASA’s Glenn Research Center posted on X on 4 November 2026: "We’re taking quantum communications to new heights! ✈️ Late last month, @NASA researchers made history when they successfully sent tiny light particles, or photons, between an aircraft and a ground station over a quantum channel, the first time this has been achieved in the U.S." The post does not name the aircraft type, the ground-station location beyond the Glenn context, or publish a link to a formal nasa.gov release.

LinkedIn corroboration, carefully attributed. On 22 October 2026, Carolyn Mercer wrote on LinkedIn that she "Got to witness NASA’s first air-to-ground quantum entanglement demonstration this afternoon at the NASA Glenn Research Center. This technology is fundamental to future science missions that will explore the universe via entangled sensor networks." Mercer’s post credits Margaret Nazario’s team and Azlin Biaggi-Labiosa for funding vision. Note the wording difference: Glenn’s X post says photons were sent "over a quantum channel"; Mercer calls what she witnessed a "quantum entanglement demonstration." This desk is not treating those two phrases as interchangeable quotes.

No nasa.gov press release found. A search for a matching November 2026 nasa.gov news release describing this specific air-to-ground quantum photon / entanglement flight did not turn up a public press page at the time of writing. Until NASA publishes a formal release with methods, dates, aircraft, link distance and measured metrics, the primary public claims remain Glenn’s X post and Mercer’s LinkedIn note. Readers should treat performance numbers that may circulate second-hand as unverified unless they appear in a NASA document.

Programme context, not this flight’s proof. Glenn maintains a Quantum Information Systems for Networking and Sensing research page that describes the centre’s broader QIS work. Earlier Twin Otter quantum-key-distribution flight experiments and classical PC-12 4K laser video demos toward the ISS are separate, older or different programmes. Do not read this November X claim as a re-announcement of those classical optical or earlier QKD flights.

Analysis. If independently documented, an air-to-ground quantum optical link from a US aircraft would matter for future entangled sensing and space-networking roadmaps Glenn has discussed in general terms. What is public today does not yet include peer-reviewed results, a nasa.gov release, bit-error or entanglement-fidelity figures, or a clear statement that the November X "quantum channel" flight is identical to the October LinkedIn "entanglement demonstration." Photon Dispatch is reporting the attributed claims and the documentation gap—not confirming a completed NASA milestone beyond those sources.

What to watch. A formal Glenn or NASA HQ release, flight-test paper, or dataset naming the aircraft, range, wavelength and measured quantum metrics would let outsiders evaluate the claim. Until then, the story rests on NASA Glenn’s X wording about photons over a quantum channel and Mercer’s LinkedIn description of an air-to-ground quantum entanglement demonstration at Glenn.

title: IonQ Partners with QuantumCT for 150+ Hours of Trapped-Ion Cloud Access in Connecticut
summary: IonQ announced a partnership with QuantumCT on 4 Nov 2026 that provides more than 150 hours of cloud runtime on IonQ trapped-ion systems for Connecticut universities, labs, startups and enterprises.
body: IonQ has partnered with QuantumCT, Connecticut's statewide quantum initiative anchored by the University of Connecticut and Yale University, to expand access to IonQ's trapped-ion quantum computers. The company announced the deal on X on 4 November: "We're partnering with @CTquantum, Connecticut's statewide initiative anchored by @UConn and @Yale, to accelerate quantum innovation and expand access to our trapped-ion quantum computers. The agreement includes more than 150 hours of cloud runtime for Connecticut's universities,"

What the contract covers. According to IonQ's news release, QuantumCT will purchase access to IonQ's trapped-ion systems on behalf of Connecticut-based, quantum-focused organisations. Participating universities, research laboratories, startups and enterprises will use the cloud resources for work spanning quantum algorithms, optimisation, materials science and workforce development. The contract includes more than 150 hours of cloud runtime and is framed as moving Connecticut's quantum community from exploration to application.

Quantum Computing Report summarised the same partnership as statewide trapped-ion cloud access for the QuantumCT network. QuantumCT is supported by a coalition of industry, government and academic partners that aims to position Connecticut as a national hub for quantum research, talent and commercialisation, IonQ's release says.

College Park, Maryland–based IonQ presented the agreement as compute procurement rather than a hardware installation in Connecticut. Access is through IonQ's cloud, so participating groups run jobs on IonQ's trapped-ion machines remotely. That model matters for universities and startups that want scheduled runtime without owning a cryogenic or vacuum system on campus.

Separate from the Elisity deal. This partnership is distinct from IonQ's completed Elisity acquisition covered elsewhere on Photon Dispatch. The QuantumCT agreement is about shared compute hours for Connecticut organisations, not a security-company purchase. Readers should not conflate the two announcements even though both landed around early November 2026.

The release does not publish a contract dollar value, a complete roster of every participating lab, or a timetable for when the 150-plus hours will be consumed. Those omissions are normal for partnership launch notes, but they also mean outsiders cannot yet measure utilisation or cost per hour from the public materials alone.

Trapped-ion hardware is IonQ's core computing pitch: ions held in electromagnetic traps and manipulated with lasers, accessed here as cloud runtime rather than as on-premise racks in Connecticut. QuantumCT's role is intermediary buyer and coordinator for organisations in its network, according to IonQ's description of the purchase.

Workforce development sits alongside algorithms and materials science in the stated focus areas. That suggests some of the hours may support teaching and training as well as research papers, though the release does not allocate the 150-plus hours among those uses. Any breakdown would have to come from QuantumCT or the universities later.

What to watch. The public figure to track is the "more than 150 hours" of runtime and which Connecticut groups actually consume it. Whether the hours accelerate published research, student training or commercial prototypes will show up in later QuantumCT, UConn, Yale and startup updates rather than in the launch post alone. For Photon Dispatch readers, the story is regional access to trapped-ion cloud time—not a new IonQ chip announcement.

title: IonQ Completes $1.15 Billion All-Stock Acquisition of Elisity
summary: IonQ has closed its all-stock purchase of Zero Trust security company Elisity, issuing $1.15 billion in common stock, with up to $150 million more tied to revenue milestones.
body: IonQ has completed its acquisition of Elisity, a Zero Trust network security company, in an all-stock deal, the quantum computing company said on 4 November. IonQ announced the closing on X: "Today, IonQ completed its acquisition of @ElisityInc. Security has always been about protecting what matters most, and quantum makes that more urgent."

The terms. According to IonQ's press release, IonQ issued $1.15 billion of consideration in common stock at closing under the merger agreement. The sellers may earn up to a further $150 million based on Elisity's performance against revenue milestones through January 2028. That extra amount is contingent and was not paid at closing.

What Elisity does. Elisity helps organisations discover the devices connected to their networks, understand network risk and enforce identity-based Zero Trust policies, an approach that does not automatically trust anything just because it is inside the network. IonQ says it will combine this with its post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) products, so customers can use Elisity's view of their networks to decide where to deploy quantum-safe protection first.

The pitch targets "Harvest Now, Decrypt Later" attacks, where encrypted data is stolen today in the hope that a future quantum computer can break it. "Enterprise and government organizations will now be able to draw on one security architecture to contain attacks operating at machine speed today, and protect sensitive information against future quantum threats," IonQ chairman and CEO Niccolo de Masi said in the release.

Customers and leadership. The release says Elisity has more than 100 established enterprise deployments and will continue to serve customers under its current leadership, with existing deployments and identity policies carried forward. Elisity CEO James Winebrenner said the company would "extend the Elisity platform customers already use to help them prepare for post-quantum cryptography."

What to watch. The deal pushes IonQ further into security, alongside its computing and networking businesses. Whether the combined products win new customers, and whether Elisity hits the revenue milestones behind the $150 million earnout, will become clearer over the next two years.

title: Alice & Bob says 22,593 cat qubits could factor RSA-2048 in 3.14 days, in a new estimate
summary: Alice & Bob's new preprint estimates that a fault-tolerant machine built from its cat qubits could factor RSA-2048 with 22,593 physical qubits in 3.14 days. It is a resource estimate on paper, not a demonstration, and it assumes hardware no one has built yet.
body: Short answer: Alice & Bob, the Paris- and Boston-based company building superconducting "cat qubit" processors, estimates that a machine on its architecture could factor a 2048-bit RSA number with 22,593 physical qubits running for 3.14 days. The figure comes from a ten-author preprint posted to the IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive (2026/2665) on 28 October, which the company described in a blog post as "about 23 000 physical qubits and about three days to break RSA-2048." It is a resource estimate, not an attack run on real hardware.

A cat qubit stores information in a superconducting resonator holding many photons. Alice & Bob's design suppresses bit flips, where a qubit's 0 turns into 1 or the reverse, in the hardware itself, so the error-correcting code layered on top only has to catch phase flips. That is why the company can claim far fewer physical qubits per logical qubit than designs that must correct both kinds of error. For the difference between the two, see our explainer on what a logical qubit is.

According to Quantum Brief, the company credits three changes for the lower count: the cat qubits themselves, LDPC-cat codes published in 2024 that replace the repetition code used in its 2023 estimate, and a rebuilt adder that runs at a steady clock instead of pausing to wait on error-correction results. The switch to LDPC-cat codes alone took the RSA-2048 count from 49,649 to 22,593, according to Alice & Bob's release.

The headline number rests on four stated assumptions: an error-correction cycle of 1 microsecond, a 10-microsecond reaction time for the classical decoder, a phase-flip probability of 5×10<sup>-4</sup>, and no bit flips at all. Alice & Bob's notes to editors say zero bit flips is equivalent to a bit-flip time of about a century, and that if bit flips arrived about once an hour, RSA-2048 would need roughly 45,000 qubits.

The design can also trade size for speed. Spread across 610,530 cat qubits in ten machines, the RSA-2048 job would take about 1.25 hours, while 21,188 qubits would stretch it to 8.08 days, according to the paper's trade-off table as reported by Quantum Brief. The same paper puts the 256-bit elliptic-curve discrete logarithm, which underpins ECDSA signatures and ECDH key exchange, at no more than 29,588 physical qubits and 61.8 minutes.

For context, Craig Gidney and Martin Ekerå put RSA-2048 at about 20 million physical qubits in 2019, and Gidney, at Google Quantum AI, brought it below one million in 2025, figures Alice & Bob cites in its own post. The company says its new figure needs about 40 times fewer physical qubits than Gidney's 2025 estimate, under different hardware assumptions. In October Iceberg Quantum put the figure at about 48,000 physical qubits for its own architecture; see our report on Pinnacle 1.2. The Quantum Insider also covered the estimate.
analysis: The estimate is detailed engineering on paper, but the gap between paper and hardware is the whole story. The largest chip Alice & Bob described in its 20 October results from France's PROQCIMA programme had 12 qubits, and the company itself reported "a logical error rate not yet below threshold," as Quantum Brief notes. The no-bit-flip assumption is also well beyond what the company has measured on a single cat qubit. Estimates from different companies rest on different hardware assumptions, so a lower number is not directly comparable to a surface-code figure from Google.

What the trend does support is the advice that already exists. Each new estimate has cut the projected machine size, which strengthens the case for the timetable in NIST IR 8547: RSA and elliptic-curve public-key algorithms deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035. Organisations planning that move can start with the standards that already exist; our explainer covers what ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA each do. Nothing in this paper means RSA-2048 can be broken today.
disclaimer: Figures are Alice & Bob's own resource estimates from a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, and they have not been independently verified. This is not a security assessment of any particular system.

title: What is FN-DSA? NIST's Falcon signature standard, and why FIPS 206 isn't published yet
summary: Checked on csrc.nist.gov on 2 November 2026, FIPS 206 for FN-DSA, NIST's planned Falcon-based signature standard, still has no public draft.
body: Short answer: FN-DSA is the name NIST plans to give FIPS 206, a digital-signature standard based on the Falcon scheme. Checked on csrc.nist.gov on 2 November 2026, FIPS 206 has not been published, not even as an initial public draft. NIST's post-quantum cryptography project page says the Falcon algorithm "was selected for ongoing standardization" and "that process is underway," and the agency's selected-algorithms list still marks Falcon "FIPS coming soon."

NIST picked Falcon in July 2022, alongside CRYSTALS-Dilithium and SPHINCS+, as one of the algorithms it would standardize after its multi-year public competition. Dilithium and SPHINCS+ became FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) in August 2024; Falcon was held back for its own standard, which NIST calls FN-DSA. The other post-quantum standard still pending is HQC, a backup encryption algorithm NIST selected in March 2025; see PhotonDispatch's explainer on what HQC does. Our explainer on what ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA each do covers the three standards that did ship in 2024.

NIST has described the FIPS 206 draft as close to finished without publishing it. Writing on NIST's public pqc-forum mailing list on 28 August 2025, Dustin Moody, who leads the agency's post-quantum cryptography project, said the draft was "essentially completed on our end" and had gone up for internal approval to publish. He said the draft keeps Falcon's randomized signing rather than switching to a deterministic variant, and that NIST adjusted the Gaussian sampler used in key generation after consulting the Falcon submission team.

The delay traces to how Falcon signs. Falcon's reference design samples from a Gaussian distribution using floating-point arithmetic, which is hard to make both fast and resistant to timing side channels that could leak secret-key information. In correspondence posted to pqc-forum in September 2025, NIST said it would let implementers use fixed-point arithmetic for one step of key generation, but ruled out fixed-point signing because it would need roughly 256 bits per value. For signing itself, FIPS 206 will allow either native or software-emulated floating point, and NIST said it secured permission from IEEE to reprint the needed parts of the IEEE 754-2019 floating-point standard so FIPS 206 would not require a separate paid reference.

FN-DSA will sit alongside, not replace, the two 2024 signature standards, and all three rest on different math. ML-DSA is built on structured, or module, lattices and signs using the Fiat-Shamir-with-aborts technique from its CRYSTALS-Dilithium submission. SLH-DSA is a stateless hash-based scheme descended from SPHINCS+, which only relies on the security of its underlying hash function. FN-DSA is also lattice-based, but over NTRU lattices rather than module lattices, using the hash-and-sign framework of Gentry, Peikert and Vaikuntanathan with a technique Falcon's designers call fast Fourier sampling, according to the Falcon specification. NIST's 2030 and 2035 migration deadlines, covered in PhotonDispatch's report on IR 8547, apply to the older algorithms FN-DSA and its two finished siblings are meant to eventually replace; see our policy coverage for the wider transition.

Falcon's appeal is size. In the algorithm's pre-standardization specification, Falcon-512, roughly matched to NIST's security category 1, produces a 666-byte signature with an 897-byte public key; Falcon-1024, at category 5, produces a 1,280-byte signature with a 1,793-byte public key. For comparison, NIST's FIPS 204 specifies a 2,420-byte signature and a 1,312-byte public key for the smallest ML-DSA parameter set, ML-DSA-44, and FIPS 205 specifies a 7,856-byte signature but only a 32-byte public key for the smallest SLH-DSA parameter set. These Falcon figures are from the designers' own specification, published before NIST finished adapting the algorithm into FIPS 206, so the final numbers in the standard could still move slightly.

Smaller signatures matter most where many of them accumulate: a TLS handshake that chains several certificates, a DNSSEC response, a firmware update that gets re-verified at every boot, or a device with a narrow radio link. NIST has not given a publication date for FIPS 206. Outside trackers that monitor the agency's own pages put a final standard in late 2026 or early 2027, but that is their estimate, not a NIST commitment, so check csrc.nist.gov directly before planning around it.
analysis: FN-DSA looks like a near-complete standard, not an abandoned one: NIST says the specification text is largely finished and the holdup is about implementation safety, chiefly making floating-point signing resistant to timing side channels, not a weakness found in Falcon's underlying math. Organizations that need a post-quantum signature today should keep using ML-DSA or SLH-DSA, as NIST already recommends. FN-DSA is worth watching for size-constrained deployments once FIPS 206 is final, not a reason to delay adopting the standards that already exist.
disclaimer: This article describes standards NIST has published or is developing. It is not legal advice and not a configuration guide for any particular system. Figures for FN-DSA are from the pre-standardization Falcon specification and may change before FIPS 206 is finalized.

title: What is HQC? NIST's backup to ML-KEM, explained
summary: According to NIST, HQC is a code-based encryption algorithm chosen in March 2025 as a backup to ML-KEM, with a final standard expected in 2027.
body: Short answer: HQC is a post-quantum encryption algorithm that NIST selected on 11 March 2025 as a backup for ML-KEM, the main standard for general encryption. It is built on different mathematics, error-correcting codes rather than structured lattices, so that a weakness found in ML-KEM would not take both down at once.

Some background first. In August 2024 NIST finalized three post-quantum standards. FIPS 203 covers ML-KEM, a key-encapsulation mechanism: a way for two parties to agree a shared secret key over a public network. FIPS 204 and FIPS 205 cover digital signatures. Our explainer on what ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA each do goes through them one by one.

HQC fills a narrow role. NIST says it is not intended to replace ML-KEM, which remains the recommended choice for general encryption. Dustin Moody, who heads NIST's Post-Quantum Cryptography project, said organizations should keep migrating to the standards finalized in 2024, and that NIST wanted "a backup standard that is based on a different math approach than ML-KEM."

The difference in mathematics is the whole point. ML-KEM is built around structured lattices. HQC is built around error-correcting codes, an idea NIST notes has been used in information security for decades. If a new attack, quantum or classical, turned out to weaken lattice schemes, a code-based scheme would not automatically fall with it.

There is a cost. Moody said HQC is a lengthier algorithm than ML-KEM and demands more computing resources, but its clean and secure operation convinced reviewers it would be a worthy backup. HQC was the only algorithm standardized from NIST's fourth round of candidates, which began with four algorithms meriting further study.

On timing, NIST said in March 2025 that it planned to issue a draft standard incorporating HQC in about a year, with a finalized standard expected in 2027. Check NIST's Computer Security Resource Center for the current status of that draft before relying on a date. For the wider migration deadlines, see our piece on NIST IR 8547 and the 2030 and 2035 dates.
analysis: For most organizations HQC changes nothing today: NIST's own advice is to keep moving to ML-KEM and the 2024 signature standards. Its value is insurance. Having a second key-establishment standard built on unrelated mathematics gives a fallback if lattice cryptanalysis improves, which is the same logic NIST applied when it described SLH-DSA as a backup signature method. Selecting HQC is not a sign that ML-KEM has been broken.
disclaimer: This article describes NIST announcements. It is not legal advice and not a configuration guide for any particular system.

title: Harvest now, decrypt later: why encrypted data is already at risk from quantum computers
summary: Harvest now, decrypt later means recording encrypted traffic today and breaking it once a large quantum computer exists. Here is how the threat works and why it sets the migration clock.
body: Short answer: "Harvest now, decrypt later" describes an attacker who copies encrypted data today, stores it, and waits until a large enough quantum computer can break the public key cryptography that protected it. The data does not need to be decrypted now to be at risk now. That is why governments ask organisations to move to post-quantum cryptography years before such a machine exists.

Most internet encryption uses two layers. A public key method such as RSA or elliptic curve Diffie Hellman agrees a shared secret, and a symmetric cipher such as AES then encrypts the actual data with that secret. A sufficiently large quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could recover the secret from the recorded key exchange, and with it the data. Symmetric ciphers are much less exposed; the main defence there is using adequately long keys.

The risk depends on how long the data must stay secret. If information will still matter in ten or fifteen years, such as health records, state secrets, long term contracts or intellectual property, then traffic captured today could become readable within its useful life. Short lived data, such as a one time login code, matters far less.

The answer is to change the key exchange, not to wait. NIST published FIPS 203 in August 2024, which standardises ML-KEM, a key encapsulation mechanism designed to resist quantum attack. Our guide to ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA explains what each standard does. Many deployments use a hybrid approach that combines a classical exchange with ML-KEM, so the connection stays secure if either one holds.

Official timelines reflect this. NIST's draft report IR 8547 proposes deprecating quantum vulnerable public key algorithms at the 112 bit security level after 2030 and disallowing them after 2035; we covered it in our report on the draft. The UK's NCSC sets milestones of 2028 for discovery and planning, 2031 for priority migrations and 2035 for completing migration.
analysis: Opinion: Nobody can say when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer will arrive, and estimates have moved repeatedly. Harvest now, decrypt later turns that uncertainty into a simple planning question: how long must this data stay private, and how long will migration take? If the sum reaches past the earliest plausible date, the work should already be under way.
disclaimer: This is a general explainer, not security advice for any specific system. Dates are from the NIST and NCSC documents linked below.

title: Quantum error correction basics: syndromes, thresholds and why overhead matters
summary: Quantum error correction detects errors through parity-check measurements and, below a hardware threshold, makes encoded qubits more reliable as codes grow, according to the research literature.
body: Short answer: Quantum error correction protects quantum information by encoding it redundantly across many qubits, repeatedly measuring parity checks that reveal errors without revealing the data, and using a classical decoder to work out and undo the most likely errors. It only helps if the hardware's error rate is below a threshold, and it costs many physical qubits per protected qubit.

Quantum computers suffer two basic kinds of error: bit flips, which swap 0 and 1, and phase flips, which change the sign relationship in a superposition. Real noise is continuous, but measuring a code's parity checks forces it into one of a discrete set of outcomes, so correcting bit flips and phase flips is enough to handle general errors. Gottesman's introduction to the field sets out this 'discretisation of errors' and the stabilizer formalism most codes are built on.

The pattern of parity-check results is called the syndrome. In each round of error correction, helper qubits interact with groups of data qubits and are measured; a change in the syndrome flags an error nearby. A decoder, which is ordinary classical software or hardware, takes the stream of syndromes and decides which correction to apply. It has to keep pace with the machine. Google Quantum AI's 2024 Nature paper reported an average decoder latency of 63 microseconds at distance 5 with a 1.1-microsecond cycle time, running for up to a million cycles.

The threshold theorem is what makes the approach worthwhile. In the 1990s Dorit Aharonov and Michael Ben-Or, among others, showed that if each component's error probability is below some constant threshold, arbitrarily long quantum computations can be made reliable with only polylogarithmic overhead, by using codes within codes. Modern surface-code estimates put the threshold for realistic noise near 1% per operation, according to Fowler and colleagues' 2012 review.

Overhead is the catch. Fowler's review estimated that useful fault-tolerant machines would need very large numbers of physical qubits, because each logical qubit uses hundreds to thousands of them and some operations need extra resources, such as 'magic states', to complete a universal gate set. Lower physical error rates, better decoders and more efficient codes all shrink that overhead, which is why researchers track the logical error rate per cycle and how fast it falls as codes grow.

Experiments have begun to show the expected behaviour. Google reported in 2024 that its distance-7 surface-code memory on the Willow chip had an error rate of 0.143% per cycle, and that each increase of two in code distance cut the logical error rate by a factor of 2.14. The same paper noted that rare correlated error events, roughly once an hour, limited its longest repetition-code runs.
analysis: Error correction has moved from theory to engineering, but the open questions are practical: how to handle correlated errors, how to decode fast enough at scale, and how many physical qubits a useful machine will really need. Resource estimates differ widely depending on hardware assumptions, so a single number for 'qubits needed' should be read with its assumptions attached.

title: What is a logical qubit, and why do quantum computers need them?
summary: A logical qubit is one unit of quantum information spread across many physical qubits so that errors can be detected and corrected, as described in surface-code research.
body: Short answer: A logical qubit is a qubit built out of many physical qubits. The quantum information is spread across the group in a pattern, called an error-correcting code, so that errors on individual physical qubits can be detected and fixed without reading out, and destroying, the information itself.

Physical qubits, whether superconducting circuits, trapped ions or neutral atoms, are fragile. Heat, stray fields and imperfect control pulses flip or blur their states, and today's best hardware still makes errors far more often than long, useful algorithms are expected to tolerate. A logical qubit is the field's answer: rather than waiting for perfect hardware, it adds redundancy.

The idea can't simply copy classical backup. The no-cloning theorem says an unknown quantum state cannot be copied, and measuring a qubit directly collapses it. Error-correcting codes get around this by measuring only joint properties of groups of qubits, called stabilizers or parity checks. Those checks reveal whether, and roughly where, an error happened, but say nothing about the encoded value, as Daniel Gottesman's widely used introduction to the subject explains.

The most studied design is the surface code, in which physical qubits sit on a two-dimensional grid and neighbouring groups are checked over and over in rounds. Austin Fowler and colleagues' 2012 review describes how logical qubits are formed on such a grid and how operations between them are carried out. The size of a surface-code logical qubit is set by its code distance, d: a distance-d code needs on the order of 2d² physical qubits including the measurement helpers, and can correct any combination of fewer than about d/2 errors.

Bigger is only better if the hardware is good enough. Below a hardware error rate called the threshold, each step up in code distance makes the logical qubit more reliable; above it, adding qubits makes things worse. In a paper published in Nature in December 2024, Google Quantum AI reported a 101-qubit distance-7 surface-code memory on its Willow processor with an error rate of 0.143% per error-correction cycle, and said the logical error rate fell by a factor of 2.14 each time the distance grew by two. The team also reported that the logical memory outlived its best physical qubit by a factor of 2.4.

Other hardware approaches use the same concept. A Harvard-led team reported in Nature in 2023 a neutral-atom processor that ran circuits with up to 48 logical qubits using a small error-detecting code, and improved a logical two-qubit gate by moving from a distance-3 to a distance-7 surface code.
analysis: Logical qubit counts are now a common headline number, but they aren't directly comparable between announcements. Codes differ in how many errors they can correct, some experiments detect errors without correcting them, and a logical qubit used only as a memory is not the same as one that can run a full set of gates. When reading a claim, look for the code distance, the logical error rate per cycle or per operation, and whether the result has been peer reviewed.

title: NIST says quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035
summary: According to NIST IR 8547, published 27 October 2026, quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035.
body: Short answer: On 27 October 2026 the US National Institute of Standards and Technology published NIST IR 8547, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards. NIST says it will deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow its use under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035.

The report is dated October 2026. Its publication history says the NIST Editorial Review Board approved it on 21 October 2026, and both NIST's news post and the Computer Security Resource Center list 27 October 2026. It is the agency's plan for moving off public-key methods that a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer could break, toward the post-quantum standards NIST finished in 2024: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) for key establishment, and FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) for signatures. Dustin Moody, the NIST mathematician who leads the project, said there is "not one strategy that fits all use cases".

For signatures, NIST's table covers ECDSA, EdDSA and RSA as specified in FIPS 186, at the parameter sets it still treats as approved: at least 112 bits of classical security for ECDSA and RSA, and at least 128 bits for EdDSA. Each is marked deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035. The same window applies to quantum-vulnerable key establishment in Special Publications 800-56A and 800-56B: finite-field and elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman and MQV, and RSA key establishment, again from 112 bits of classical security upward. NIST says this replaces an older plan, in SP 800-57 Part 1, to disallow public-key schemes offering 112 bits of security on 1 January 2031.

National Security Memorandum 10 still names 2035 as the target for finishing the migration across federal systems, the report says. Executive Order 14412 and OMB Memorandum M-26-15, as the report describes them, pull the most sensitive systems forward: high-value assets and high-impact systems are to adopt post-quantum key establishment by 31 December 2030 and post-quantum digital signatures by 31 December 2031. NIST says the broader 2030-2035 window does not relax those earlier deadlines. The report also says Executive Order 14306 and the same OMB memo require agencies to support TLS 1.3 no later than 2 January 2030.

NIST says ML-KEM, specified in FIPS 203, is at present the only approved post-quantum key-establishment scheme based on public-key cryptography, and it recommends the ML-KEM-768 parameter set as the default. HQC has been chosen for a future standard; NIST says it becomes an approved scheme after that standard is published. Symmetric cryptography is on a different footing: the report says approved symmetric primitives with at least 128 bits of classical security are believed to meet at least Category 1 on NIST's post-quantum scale, while a few symmetric standards at the 112-bit level are to be disallowed in 2030.
analysis: In the report's own glossary, a deprecated algorithm may still be used if the data owner accepts the risk, while a disallowed algorithm is no longer allowed for the stated purpose. The December 2030 and December 2031 dates apply to the sensitive federal systems the report names. They are not, on the text of IR 8547, an automatic cutoff for every deployment of RSA.
disclaimer: Dates and requirements are NIST's, as stated in IR 8547 and the agency's 27 October 2026 news post. This is not legal advice, and it is not a finding about any particular system.

title: IQM says Emerald entangled all 54 qubits, with a GHZ fidelity of 0.516
summary: IQM says its Emerald cloud system prepared a 54-qubit GHZ state at fidelity 0.516 with readout-error mitigation, just above 0.5.
body: Short answer: IQM Quantum Computers said on 29 October 2026 that its cloud-accessible Emerald processor had entangled all 54 qubits on the chip at the same time. IQM measured a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger fidelity of 0.516 for the full chip when readout-error mitigation was applied, and 0.515 for a 40-qubit version of the same test without that mitigation. The company says both numbers sit above 0.500, the line it uses to separate genuine multipartite entanglement from noise.

The state was prepared across the whole Emerald chip, IQM says, by an automated routine that picks two-qubit gates and the order they run in, weighing gate quality against how long other qubits sit idle. Craig Ciesla, IQM's chief technology officer, said the result "came down to being smarter about how we prepare the state".

IQM says the demonstration follows about a year of hardware and calibration work: a revised calibration method, an updated gate set, and continued use of dynamical decoupling and qubit selection. The company says those changes cut the error rate of quantum operations in the processor by up to 50 percent. It also says that, before this run, a comparable demonstration on Emerald could reliably use on the order of 30 qubits inside a single algorithm, and that cloud customers can now call on that same full-chip performance.

The announcement was issued through Business Wire at 3:00 a.m. US Eastern time and datelined Espoo, Finland. IQM describes itself as a superconducting quantum-computing company founded in 2018 and listed on Nasdaq under the symbol IQMX.
IQM says the preparation routine is part of a wider effort to automate how its machines are operated and tuned, including calibration work the company describes as AI-driven.
analysis: The 54-qubit fidelity includes readout-error mitigation and the 40-qubit figure does not, so the two results are not a like-for-like picture of scaling. A fidelity of 0.516 is only slightly above the 0.5 line IQM cites. The figures are the company's, given in a press release rather than in a paper linked from that release.
disclaimer: Fidelity figures, the error-rate claim and the comparison with earlier Emerald runs are IQM's own statements and have not been independently verified. IQM Quantum Computers is listed on Nasdaq (IQMX). This is not investment advice.

title: What ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA each do in NIST's post-quantum standards
summary: According to NIST, FIPS 203, 204 and 205, effective 14 August 2024, cover key establishment (ML-KEM) and two signature methods (ML-DSA and SLH-DSA).
body: Short answer: The three post-quantum standards NIST finalized in August 2024 do different jobs. FIPS 203, ML-KEM, is for agreeing a shared secret key. FIPS 204, ML-DSA, is the primary standard for digital signatures. FIPS 205, SLH-DSA, is a second signature method, built on different mathematics, which NIST describes as a backup.

A key-encapsulation mechanism lets two parties derive a shared secret over a public network. NIST says ML-KEM, taken from the CRYSTALS-Kyber submission, is the main standard for general encryption, citing comparatively small keys and speed. ML-DSA, from CRYSTALS-Dilithium, is for signatures that tie a message to a signer and show whether it was changed. SLH-DSA, from SPHINCS+, is also a signature scheme. NIST says it uses a different mathematical approach from ML-DSA and is there as a backup should a weakness in ML-DSA turn up.

The Secretary of Commerce approved FIPS 203, 204 and 205, and the Federal Register notice (89 FR 66052) makes them effective on 14 August 2024. NIST's news post of 13 August 2024 said the documents include the algorithms, instructions for implementing them and the uses they are meant for, and that they were ready to use. Dustin Moody, who leads the project, said "full integration will take time."

In 2022 NIST selected four algorithms to standardize: CRYSTALS-Kyber, CRYSTALS-Dilithium, SPHINCS+ and FALCON. The August 2024 post said a draft based on FALCON, to be named FN-DSA, was still planned. NIST IR 8547, published in October 2026, says the agency is still developing a FIPS for a signature algorithm derived from FALCON, as a further alternative, and it recommends ML-KEM-768 as the default parameter set for FIPS 203. The 2030 and 2035 transition dates are set out in PhotonDispatch's report on that roadmap.

NIST says the new algorithms rest on math problems intended to resist both conventional computers and quantum computers, unlike factoring and discrete logarithms, which underlie widely used schemes such as RSA and elliptic-curve signatures. The agency describes the three 2024 standards as the primary tools for general encryption and for signatures, and says further algorithms are backups rather than a reason to wait.
analysis: Publishing a standard is not the same thing as finishing a migration, and it is not evidence that a quantum computer can break public-key encryption today. NIST's August 2024 announcement described a machine with that capability as a future possibility. Describing SLH-DSA as a backup was a design choice NIST stated at the time, not a report that ML-DSA had failed.
disclaimer: This article describes standards NIST has published. It is not legal advice and not a configuration guide for any particular system.

title: Quantinuum says Helios hit 99.9995% logical fidelity, a tenfold error-correction record
summary: Quantinuum says its Helios trapped-ion computer reached 99.9995% logical fidelity with a color code, about five errors per million operations.
body: Short answer: Quantinuum announced on 19 October 2026 that its Helios commercial quantum computer achieved a logical fidelity of 99.9995%, which the company says equals about five errors in a million operations. Quantinuum calls it a world record for quantum error correction.

According to the company, the error rate is 10 times lower than the record Quantinuum itself set in September 2026 and 100 times lower than the best published result on any other hardware type, which it says was reported by Google Quantum AI on a superconducting system.

The result used a well-known error-correcting scheme called a color code. Quantinuum says logical errors fell exponentially as it increased the code distance, with each tested step cutting the remaining errors by what it calls a record factor of 12.

The trade-off is qubit overhead. On Helios, Quantinuum says its earlier Helix code used 10 physical qubits per logical qubit, while the color code used up to 37, in exchange for lower logical error rates. Both studies ran on the same hardware.
Quantinuum says the accuracy is now within the target range for Apollo, its planned universal fault-tolerant quantum computer, which it expects to be available by 2029.
analysis: Comparisons of logical fidelity across companies depend on the codes, operations and benchmarks used. The figures here are Quantinuum's own and have not been independently replicated.

title: Google shows magic state cultivation on Willow, cutting errors about 40x
summary: Google Quantum AI says magic state cultivation worked on its Willow chip, cutting errors about 40-fold and yielding T-states at 99.99% logical fidelity.
body: Short answer: Google Quantum AI said on 15 October 2026 that it has demonstrated "magic state cultivation" on its Willow processor, reducing errors about 40 times compared with uncultivated states and producing T-states with a logical fidelity of 99.99%, which it calls a record. The work was published in Science the same day, according to Google.

Magic states are special quantum states needed to run the full set of operations that make a quantum computer universal. Google says producing high-quality, error-corrected magic states is so costly that some estimates put up to 95% of a machine's capacity into making them, and each one can only be used once.

Cultivation, developed in a 2024 theory paper by Google researchers Craig Gidney, Noah Shutty and Cody Jones, works like a filter: a noisy state is injected into a small patch of the chip and checked with coordinated measurements, and flawed attempts are thrown away, according to Google's description.

Google says the team also had to invent a new benchmarking method after lab noise from equipment drift and temperature changes undermined its usual measurement technique. It also moved purified states from a distance-3 color code into a distance-5 surface code, showing the states can survive the transfer on its hardware.
Google says cultivation still has to be shown at a larger scale and that plenty of technical challenges remain before it is practical.

title: Iceberg Quantum cuts its RSA-2048 factoring estimate to about 48,000 qubits in simulations
summary: Iceberg Quantum's Pinnacle 1.2 says simulations show RSA-2048 factoring could need about 48,000 physical qubits and roughly a day under its best assumptions.
body: Short answer: Iceberg Quantum published Pinnacle 1.2 on 22 October 2026, saying direct circuit-level simulations show its Pinnacle architecture can reach logical error rates low enough to factor a 2048-bit RSA key, at a spacetime cost about an order of magnitude lower than its Pinnacle 1.0 estimate. Under its most favourable assumptions (physical error rate of 10-4 and a 1 microsecond code cycle), the company estimates about 48,000 physical qubits and an expected runtime of 0.98 days.

The result rests on a new decoder for QLDPC error-correcting codes called Crevasse, which Iceberg says takes four microseconds on average per round of error correction. Using it, the company says it processed trillions of simulated error-correction instances and directly observed a logical error rate below one error per trillion logical qubit-cycles, without extrapolation.

Iceberg says smaller codes than it previously assumed are enough, cutting space overhead by about 40% and time overhead by about 30% versus Pinnacle 1.0. It also says it compiled and verified a complete modular exponentiation circuit, the core of Shor's factoring algorithm, and counted the operations directly.

The estimates vary widely with hardware speed and quality. Iceberg's table gives 72,000 qubits and 3.7 days at a 10<sup>-3</sup> error rate with a 1 microsecond cycle, and 714,000 qubits (29 days) to 2.1 million qubits (32 days) with a 1 millisecond cycle. For fixed-connectivity superconducting systems, its Frozen Pinnacle variant comes to about 99,000 qubits and 5.0 days, the company says.
analysis: These are simulations and resource estimates, not a demonstration on hardware. No machine of this size exists today. The figures are best read as one more input to post-quantum cryptography migration planning.

UKRI says the funding is part of the government's mission to make the UK a world leader in quantum sensing by 2030, which it says is backed by up to £2 billion of investment announced earlier this year.

title: Universal Quantum Unveils Integrated Ion-Trap Processor for DLR Systems
summary: Universal Quantum says its new iQPU integrates a large trapped-ion surface, custom control electronics and modular links for two German Aerospace Center systems.
body: Universal Quantum announced its integrated quantum processing unit, or iQPU, on November 3, positioning the chip as a way to address the wiring and connectivity problems that complicate large trapped-ion computers. The UK-based company, which also operates in Hamburg, says the module will be used in two systems it is building for the German Aerospace Center, DLR. That identified destination makes the announcement more concrete than a standalone laboratory concept, although performance in those systems remains to be demonstrated.

The processor combines a trapped-ion compute surface, control electronics and chip-to-chip interfaces in one design. Universal Quantum reports an active computing area exceeding 400 square millimeters and describes it as the largest trapped-ion compute surface. The size claim is the company’s; it should not be interpreted as an independently verified ranking across every competing architecture.

The chip follows a quantum charge-coupled device approach, usually abbreviated QCCD. Instead of keeping every ion fixed in one position, the architecture moves ions among zones so qubits can be brought together for operations. That matters because quantum algorithms often require interactions between qubits that are not neighbors in a simple layout. Physical movement can offer flexible connectivity, though transport speed, heating and operation fidelity all influence whether the approach produces a practical advantage.

Universal Quantum has also integrated custom application-specific control circuitry, or ASICs, into the stack. Conventional scaling can require an increasingly awkward collection of external signal lines as more qubits are added. Bringing some switching and control closer to the processor is intended to reduce that burden. It does not eliminate the need for lasers, vacuum hardware, calibration or other supporting systems, but it addresses one important source of engineering complexity.

The third element is UQConnect, the company’s interface for linking neighboring modules. Universal Quantum says ions can move directly between modules, allowing several chips to behave as a larger system without redesigning the base unit. This is a different modularity proposition from architectures that rely entirely on optical links between separately housed quantum processors. It may simplify some operations if reliable transport between modules can be maintained at scale.

Manufacturing is another noteworthy part of the announcement. DesignQuantum reports that the iQPU is made on a 200-millimeter production line. Using an established wafer format is relevant to repeatability, process control and potential supply-chain development. Yet wafer size alone says nothing about usable chip yield or the number of working qubits delivered. Those metrics will become essential if Universal Quantum attempts to produce many identical modules.

The DLR deployment gives the project an immediate engineering test. Integrating the modules into two complete systems will require coordination among trapping hardware, electronics, control software and error-management techniques. The relevant milestones are not just successful manufacturing but stable operation, repeatable gate performance and useful multi-qubit computations across the designed connections.

Universal Quantum’s announcement arrives as developers of superconducting, trapped-ion and other architectures pursue different ways to build larger machines. There is no settled winner, and a claimed connectivity benefit must ultimately be judged alongside noise, speed, manufacturing yield and the resources required to correct errors. An ion chip with excellent routing could still face limitations elsewhere in the system.

For now, the company has disclosed a defined hardware package: a more-than-400-square-millimeter trapped-ion surface, integrated control ASICs, UQConnect interfaces and a planned role in two DLR machines. The next question is how those features perform together under sustained operation. Publishing measured gate fidelities, transport error rates and system uptime would make it possible to judge whether the integration is a practical step toward larger fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Quint Computing Raises €9.1 Million for Error-Suppressing Quantum Chips
summary: German startup Quint Computing has raised €9.1 million in a first funding round and secured a separate €2.2 million European research grant for its quantum hardware approach.
body: Erlangen-based Quint Computing announced on November 3 that it has completed a €9.1 million first financing round, led by Vsquared Ventures, to develop superconducting quantum chips designed to suppress errors at the hardware level. The startup also disclosed a separate €2.2 million European Innovation Council Pathfinder grant. The two amounts have different purposes and should not be presented as one venture-capital round. (Design Quantum)

The company says the €9.1 million investment is the largest first funding round raised by a quantum computing company in Germany. That is a company assertion, rather than a ranking independently established here. According to DesignQuantum’s report, other participants include Quantonation, Nucleus Capital, Faber, Vanagon Ventures and ZOHO.VC, along with individual industry figures such as IQM and QMill founder Mikko Möttönen.

Quint is young even by quantum-industry standards. It says it was founded in October 2025 by physicists Michael Hartmann, its chief technology officer, and Christopher Eichler, its chief executive, alongside economist Jona Stinner, its finance and operations leader. The company is a spinout from Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg and identifies with the Munich Quantum Valley ecosystem. Its roots in academic research are significant because its strategy depends on changing the behavior of the physical qubit rather than merely adding more software-level correction on top.

Error correction is one of quantum computing’s hardest scaling problems. Quantum information is vulnerable to noise, and building one reliable logical qubit may require many imperfect physical qubits plus repeated measurements and corrective operations. Hardware that reduces a particularly costly error channel could lower the overhead required for a useful machine. But the degree of improvement depends on which errors are suppressed, what new errors are introduced and how the qubits behave during real computational gates.

Quint’s investment thesis is therefore more specific than a generic promise to build a quantum processor. It is betting that suppressing errors in the chip design can change the resource requirements of fault-tolerant computation. Investors will eventually need evidence from manufactured devices, not only theoretical comparisons. Useful disclosures would include measured error rates, manufacturing yield, reproducibility across devices and the effect of the design on multi-qubit operations.

The startup plans to use the new financing to expand its team, accelerate technology development and begin industrial deployment projects. DesignQuantum reports a target of roughly 40 employees by 2028, with recruiting focused on chip design, chip manufacturing, error correction and applications. For a company formed only a little more than a year ago, staffing those disciplines is itself a material operational challenge.

The €2.2 million EIC Pathfinder award adds a research-oriented funding channel alongside private investors. Public grants can support technically risky development that may not produce near-term commercial revenue, while venture money can fund company formation and the work needed to turn laboratory concepts into repeatable products. Neither funding source proves that Quint has solved fault tolerance, and neither guarantees a future commercial quantum computer.

Quint also faces a competitive field. Other superconducting developers, including Alice & Bob, are trying to engineer error behavior in hardware rather than relying exclusively on larger layers of correction. The strategies differ, but the common commercial question is whether a hardware-level advantage survives when devices are connected and operated as a processor.

The November announcement is consequential because it gives Quint named backers, a quantified funding base and a stated hiring and development plan. It is not a processor-performance announcement. The evidence that matters next will come from experimental benchmarks and from whether the company can move its designs beyond university facilities into repeatable industrial manufacturing.

title: Alice & Bob Reports Multi-Hour Bit-Flip Lifetimes on Cat-Qubit Hardware
summary: Alice & Bob has reported 44-minute average bit-flip lifetimes on a single device and multi-hour measurements on its 12-qubit Helium 2 processor, with major gate-level challenges remaining.
body: French quantum hardware developer Alice & Bob has reported unusually long idle bit-flip lifetimes in experiments on its superconducting cat-qubit technology. A technical update covered by Quantum Computing Report on November 2 describes an average 44-minute lifetime on a single-qubit device, with selected qubits on the company’s 12-qubit Helium 2 processor showing lifetimes measured in hours. The result is important for the firm’s error-correction strategy, but it does not mean that an entire quantum computation can run for hours without errors.

The single-device experiment monitored the system continuously for 61 hours and recorded 41 discrete quantum jumps. Quantum Computing Report lists a mean bit-flip lifetime of 44 minutes and a 95% confidence interval of 33 to 60 minutes, with an average occupation of 11 photons. These are statistical measurements of a specific error process during idle operation, not a general-purpose qubit coherence time.

On Helium 2, a 12-qubit processor, the reported idle bit-flip lifetimes included 189 minutes for one qubit, 252 minutes for another and 189 minutes for a third. The photon occupation in those tests ranged from 11 to 16. Those multi-hour figures indicate that the suppression effect can appear in a multi-qubit environment, although the data reported do not establish identical performance for every qubit or under every operating condition.

Cat qubits encode information in superpositions of coherent states in superconducting microwave cavities. The design uses engineered two-photon dissipation to suppress bit flips as the cat state grows. The tradeoff is that another error channel, phase flips, can become more prominent. This asymmetry is the central idea behind Alice & Bob’s approach: if one type of error is made very rare, the remaining correction problem may become simpler.

The tradeoff is visible in the company’s own measurements. Quantum Computing Report lists a phase-flip lifetime of 420 nanoseconds in a parity-decay measurement on the single-qubit device, corresponding to a single-photon T1 of 9.2 microseconds. The team also demonstrated resonant-drive Z rotations, reporting a 94.2% gate fidelity for a 26.5-nanosecond operation. Those numbers are not interchangeable with the long idle bit-flip lifetime. They illustrate why quantum-computing claims must specify which operation and error channel were measured.

The new data also connect to Alice & Bob’s earlier resource estimates for breaking RSA-2048 with Shor’s algorithm. A previous compilation discussed roughly 22,593 physical qubits under an idealized 100-year bit-flip lifetime assumption. With a more realistic once-per-hour physical bit-flip rate and an additional outer correction layer, the modeled requirement rose to roughly 45,000 qubits. The November experiments provide evidence relevant to the hour-scale assumption, not evidence that the proposed RSA-breaking computer has been built.

The next bottleneck is maintaining favorable error behavior during entangling operations. A useful fault-tolerant processor must perform repeated two-qubit gates, measure error syndromes and correct mistakes while computations proceed. Idle stability alone cannot demonstrate that capability. In particular, bias-preserving controlled-NOT operations and active logical error correction remain milestones identified in the reporting.

The significance of the result is therefore precise. Alice & Bob has produced experimental measurements that support one of the physical assumptions behind its error-correction architecture. The company has not shown that every relevant gate achieves the same suppression, that logical error rates are below useful thresholds, or that its proposed large-scale processor is imminent.

For researchers and prospective partners, the most valuable follow-up will be side-by-side data on idle and active error rates, reproducibility across larger arrays, and logical-qubit performance under a complete correction cycle. Those measurements will determine whether multi-hour protection against one error channel can translate into the much broader reliability required for commercially useful quantum computing.

title: IQM Emerald Entangles All 54 Qubits, Opening Full Processor to Cloud Users
summary: IQM Quantum Computers says its Emerald quantum processor has achieved simultaneous entanglement across all 54 qubits, marking a step toward using the entire...
body: IQM Quantum Computers says its Emerald quantum processor has achieved simultaneous entanglement across all 54 qubits, marking a step toward using the entire chip in a single quantum computation. The company says the performance demonstrated in the test is now available to customers accessing Emerald through the cloud, rather than being confined to a smaller portion of the processor.

The announcement, reported by Quantum Spectator on November 3, concerns a challenge that extends beyond the number of qubits installed on a chip: whether those qubits can operate together while preserving the quantum correlations required for a particular experiment.

A Full-Chip Entanglement Test. IQM used a Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger, or GHZ, state to assess entanglement across Emerald. This benchmark tests whether a collection of qubits can be prepared in a shared quantum state. IQM reported a fidelity of 0.516 across all 54 qubits, with readout error mitigation applied. Fidelity measures how closely the prepared state matches the intended quantum state.

The company also reported a 0.515 fidelity at 40 qubits without readout error mitigation. Both results exceeded the 0.500 threshold cited for establishing genuine multipartite entanglement. The distinction between the measurements matters: the 54-qubit figure includes mitigation of measurement errors, while the 40-qubit result does not. They should not be treated as identical testing conditions.

IQM characterized the measurements as among the strongest reported for a commercially available quantum computer. That ranking is the company's assessment, not an independently established conclusion in the Quantum Spectator report.

Why the Whole Processor Matters. According to IQM, users previously conducting a comparable demonstration on Emerald could reliably incorporate approximately 30 qubits into one algorithm. The latest demonstration shows that the processor can sustain the benchmark across its full 54-qubit complement.

That difference is important because an advertised qubit count does not automatically indicate how many qubits can participate successfully in the same circuit. As more qubits and operations are included, the processor must manage errors associated with quantum gates and time spent waiting between operations.

IQM credits an automated state-preparation routine for helping overcome those constraints. The routine evaluates available two-qubit gates and their fidelity, while also considering how long qubits remain idle. It then chooses the qubits and operation sequence intended to reduce unnecessary waiting as the entangled state is assembled.

Calibration and Error Reduction. The result follows roughly a year of hardware and calibration improvements, according to IQM. Those efforts included revised calibration methods, an improved gate set and continued use of error-reduction techniques such as dynamical decoupling.

IQM says the combined changes reduced error rates for quantum operations on the processor by up to 50%. That figure describes the company's reported improvement; it does not mean Emerald is error-free or that every quantum algorithm will see an equivalent performance gain.

The automated preparation work also fits into IQM's broader effort to make quantum-system operation less dependent on manual tuning. The company has described additional work on AI-driven calibration as part of that direction.

What Comes Next for Cloud Researchers. For customers, the immediate development is access to full-chip performance through IQM's cloud offering. Researchers can now investigate experiments that involve all 54 qubits, rather than working within the smaller usable portion previously described by the company.

The milestone should nevertheless be read precisely. Demonstrating a GHZ state across an entire chip establishes a specific kind of coordinated quantum behavior; it does not, by itself, establish an advantage over classical computers on practical workloads. Future applications will still depend on how well the processor performs across other circuits and tasks.

For now, Emerald's achievement links a measurable laboratory benchmark with expanded access for cloud users—a significant distinction in an industry where available hardware capacity and usable computational capacity are not always the same.
